concept.name: Gamma
concept.definition: Gamma is the second-order sensitivity of an option's price to the underlying's price — the rate of change of delta per unit change in the underlying. Long options have positive gamma and short options negative gamma; gamma peaks for at-the-money options near expiration.
concept.intuition: Gamma is the accelerator pedal of your delta: the higher the gamma, the faster your position turns more long as the stock rises and more short as it falls.
concept.mechanics: Gamma = d(delta)/dS = d2V/dS2; identical for calls and puts at the same strike in Black-Scholes. It measures the convexity of the option's value and the cost of re-hedging a delta-neutral book: long-gamma positions gain from realized volatility and pay theta; short-gamma positions collect theta and lose to realized volatility.
concept.formula: Gamma = d2V/dS2; Black-Scholes: Gamma = N'(d1) / (S * sigma * sqrt(T)).
concept.failure_modes: Near expiration, ATM gamma explodes, so hedges that looked adequate become useless within hours and small price jumps force large re-hedges; short-gamma books are exactly where gap moves inflict unbounded damage, and gamma estimates are model-dependent.
concept.misconceptions: Long gamma does not mean 'profits from any move' — it profits only when realized volatility exceeds the implied volatility paid for via theta. Gamma is also not a standalone position: it is inseparable from the theta cost that funds it.
concept.example: A $100-strike call with delta 0.50 and gamma 0.08 sees its delta rise to about 0.58 if the stock rises $1; a short option with gamma -0.08 must buy back 8 deltas of hedge after that same move.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OCC) — Understanding Options Greeks
